newsitem.title: CROATIA: SOCCER-MIXED FEELINGS AS ZAGREB AND BELGRADE MEET AGAIN.
newsitem.headline: SOCCER-MIXED FEELINGS AS ZAGREB AND BELGRADE MEET AGAIN.

text.p: There were mixed reactions in Croatia and Yugoslavia on Wednesday after their top soccer clubs were drawn against each other in the qualifying round of the European Cup later this month.

The draw, made in Geneva, brought together Partizan Belgrade and Croatia Zagreb in the two-legged tie, with Partizan at home in the first leg on July 23 and Zagreb the home side in the second leg a week later.
As the draw was announced there was gasps of astonishment from the audience at the Grand Casino in the Noga Hilton Hotel.

The matches will be the first between the two old rivals who regularly used to meet in the former Yugoslavian League before the break-up of that country in the wake of the bitter war in the early 1990s. Branko Bulatovic, the secretary general of the Yugoslav Soccer Association said: "We believe a fair and sportsmanlike match can be played by these two teams in Belgrade and that there will be no problems. It's interesting that out of 16 teams we drew Croatia but it is normal that this should happen one day and we do not expect any problems."
He added: "We do not expect that UEFA will ask for the matches to be played in a third country.
"As the Yugoslav Soccer Federation we can guarantee there will be no problems for the match in Belgrade and we believe there are no problems in Zagreb either."

Nenad Bjekovic, Partizan soccer club director, said: "We are the first soccer club from Yugoslavia that will play an official match with a club from Croatia. It's sport, we do not expect any problems either here or in Zagreb."
Some observers were not so optimistic with Boris Cosic, a leading Croatian soccer journalist hinting there could be trouble ahead.
"There's a big danger because I'm not sure it will be a peaceful game. There are strong emotions and it can't be safe," he said.

"The hooligans, the rebels, I think they are happy, but other people are not. The situation at the moment is that the games will be played in Belgrade and Zagreb but I'm not sure if it will stay like that or if they will be held elsewhere.
"I think it's too early to travel to Belgrade with 2,000 fans and it would be very difficult with visas and so on."
Sinisa Bozovic, a Belgrade sports commentator, said the match would be "full of tensions not linked only to sports".

The clubs, who had a long rivalry until 1991, last met on March 17 that year when they drew 0-0 in Zagreb in a Yugoslav League match. Under the rules operating in the League at that time, Zagreb won the match 4-3 on a penalty shootout.
Croatia Zagreb, then called Dinamo, was one of Yugoslavia's four top soccer clubs vying with Partizan Belgrade and Red Star Belgrade as well as Croatian rivals Hajduk Split for the title most years.

Partizan Belgrade won the old championship 14 times to Zagreb's four and Partizan were also more successful in the Yugoslav Cup, winning that trophy five times compared with Croatia's four, but Zagreb were triumphant in their only Cup Final clash, winning 3-2 in 1960.
The winners of the tie face a meeting with England's Newcastle United in the preliminary round of the competition with a place in the Champions League at stake for the winner.
